articles.title: Axe used by Jack Nicholson in The Shining for sale as part of Stanley Kubrick auction
articles.summary: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive. The axe wielded by Jack Nicholson as he delivered his chillingly manic line “Here’s Johnny!” in the 1980 horror movie The Shining is to go on sale.
body: Nicholson’s character, Jack Torrance, uses the axe to hack out an opening in a locked door protecting his terrified wife Wendy, played by Shelley Duvall. It is also the murder weapon in the killing of Scatman Crothers’ character, Dick Hallorann. One of cinema’s most famous axes could be yours for a list price of between £30,000 and £50,000.
It is one of hundreds of items in the first auction of the personal archive of The Shining’s influential director, Stanley Kubrick, who died in 1999.

The sale includes several other lots from the film, including two sky-blue dresses worn by the twin sisters Alexa and Alexie Grady. They appear in the frocks in a memorable scene when they invite Torrance’s son, Danny, to “come play with us” as he pedals on his tricycle through the corridors of the Overlook Hotel.

The boy’s trike is not part of the sale, but a clapperboard used in the film is one of four from Kubrick’s movies to go under the hammer. The others are are from 2001: A Space Odyssey, the 1975 historical drama Barry Lyndon and Kubrick’s last film, Eyes Wide Shut.
points: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive.

articles.title: ‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels
articles.summary: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore.
body: For a TV show that only ran for five years, Charlie’s Angels packs a punch like a bikini-wearing big-hair-flicking private investigator. “We never thought we’d be talking about it 50 years later,” says Jaclyn Smith, the only original Angel to make it to the end of the show’s run. Smith, 80, has now written a memoir, I Once Knew a Guy Called Charlie – she is not, you gather, the type of actor to want to distance herself from her defining project.

As I read her book, and speak to her over Zoom, she comes across as sensible, hardworking and optimistic. Also lucky: loving and supportive parents, agents who seem to appear from nowhere and offer her work, an early hit show, a gift for making friends and getting over heartbreak. Even when she was diagnosed with breast cancer more than 20 years ago, terrifying as it was, it was caught early and successfully treated. Her positive outlook seems to extend to the excesses of US TV in the 1970s and 80s (drug use on set only gets a brief mention); her three ex-husbands get off fairly lightly; and any difficulties – her OCD, the men who stalked her at the height of her fame – are not dwelled on.

articles.title: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father
articles.summary: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father.
body: M y father, Sergiu Celibidache, loved children more than anything because they are free and true to themselves. And yet, he once made a young boy wet himself when he dared to ask for an autograph, shouting at the poor child as if he had committed a federal crime because he knew there was a black market selling his signature behind his back.

I grew up a privileged child with presents from all around the world. I was spoiled – to the despair of my mother, who always tried to keep my feet on the ground. But the gifts were part of my father’s way of making up for his long absences – he was often away touring with his orchestras.

As a young boy I had very little understanding that my father was a world-renowned conductor. I always missed him terribly when he was away, and yet he was nonetheless always very present in my life, and we were close. He was generous and attentive. There were frequent speeches about the less privileged and our duty to do something for them, and he was always eager to share stories of his picturesque childhood in Iași, Romania and his many adventures after leaving home to pursue music, without any support from his family.
points: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings.
His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father.

articles.title: The Craft review – cult high-school horror a reminder of the fearless 90s
articles.summary: The 30th-anniversary rerelease of this classic tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidence. The chrysalis of 80s and 90s high-school comedy finally gave us a veritable butterfly of fear in this cult girl-power classic from 1996, co-written and directed by Andrew Fleming…
body: Robin Tunney plays Sarah, a shy, studious teen from San Francisco who suffers from depression and buried guilt about the fact that her mother died in childbirth, and from lingering resentment at her new stepmother, with whom her dad has bought her to Los Angeles for a fresh start at a new school. Something about this new arrival intrigues a clique nicknamed “the bitches of Eastwick”, led by badass goth Nancy (Fairuza Balk); she rules over her two disciples Rochelle (Rachel True) and Bonnie, played by Neve Campbell, that same year to become a scary-movie hall-of-famer for the fledgling Scream franchise.

They are devoted to “the craft” of being a witch and it is plain that Sarah too is one of their number: she has somehow alchemised her pain and fear into dark superpowers, far in excess of anything the other three can manage. Inevitably, the forces unleashed get out of control: the group find that they can kill people and take revenge on who they want; just as inevitably, a power struggle for dominance develops between the black-lipsticked Nancy and the more wholesome Sarah.
points: The 30th-anniversary rerelease of this classic tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidence.

articles.title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
articles.summary: Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, and his last book, Adam and Eve, was due to be released later this month.
body: Bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86.
In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.
The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star.
Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where his family bought a house from John Cleese's mother.

articles.title: Darius Jabloński, Kadri Kousaar and Rodrigo Susarte Make the Cut at Tallinn TV Beats Co-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Polish film and TV luminary Darius Jabloński’s spy thriller “Fortel” and Estonia’s “Stormbird” from multi-awarded Kadri Kousaar (“Magnus,” “Mother”) feature in the lineup of Tallinn’s TV Beats Co-Financing Market, running over Nov. 16-17.
body: “Never before have we welcomed that many big names and companies,” said Petri Kemppinen, co-head of TV Beats, alongside Roosa Toivonen.

This year’s crop hails from Belgium, Czechia, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, and co-production partner Canada. As underscored by Toivonen, the geographical spread mirrors TV Beats’ core which is “to act as a bridge between the Baltics, Central Eastern Europe, and the Nordics. Three territories – Czechia, Finland, and Estonia – topped the list of applications.

“Estonia is very dynamic in TV drama, and we did receive more applications than from Lithuania and Latvia,” said Toivonen who mentioned the catchy story of “Stormbird,” about a young female fugitive, under Soviet-occupied Estonia in 1949. Also from Estonia is the fast-paced YA drama “Breaking the Ice,” produced by Jevgeni Supin, who was distinguished last year with an Honorary TV Beats Producer Award.

Next to the TV Beats Co-Financing Market slate, more than 20 other top-tier series looking for additional financing, distribution and sales, will bow at ‘TV Beats Screenings’ and ‘TV Beats Coming Soon’, to be unveiled at a later date.

articles.title: Michael Douglas Weighs In on ‘Nepo Baby’ Debate, Says the Title ‘Really Pisses Me Off’
articles.summary: Michael Douglas is wading into the “nepo baby” debate. The “Wall Street” actor, who is the son of the late Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas, opened up on a recent episode of the “SmartLess” podcast and said the title “really pisses” him off.
body: His father, Kirk, died in 2020 at 103. He starred in films including “Spartacus,” “Seven Days in May,” “20,000 Leagues Under the Sea,” “Champion,” “The Bad and the Beautiful,” “Lust for Life,” “Paths of Glory” and “Lonely Are the Brave.” He earned three Oscar nominations and was awarded an honorary Oscar in 1996.

Douglas is known for his turns in “Fatal Attraction,” “Behind the Candelabra” and more films. Douglas has won one Oscar for acting and one for producing; he took home the trophy for best actor in a leading role in 1988 for “Wall Street” and best picture in 1976 as a co-producer of “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.”

articles.title: Jon Stewart’s ‘Daily Show’ Skips David Ellison-Skydance News to Take on AI
articles.summary: On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years while declining to address the major media news of the week: David Ellison’s newly-formed Skydance Corp. swallowing up Warner Bros.
body: Stewart dedicated the show entirely to AI, first ripping apart AI leaders’ empty promises of job creation, economic prosperity and its ability to cure cancer while admitting that there’s a 10-25% chance it will kill us all. Currently, however, AI is primarily being used for ICE and other surveillance, drone warfare targeting and potential dynamic pricing at places like McDonald’s.

“What are we getting in exchange for this 10-25% chance at extinction?” asked Stewart, adding, “Right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib? What a trade! I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit.”

The comedian also pushed back at President Trump allowing these AI companies to self-regulate after his recent fawning AI summit, since the Zuckerberg’s and Musk’s of the world don’t exactly have a sterling track record when it comes to playing it safe. There’s also the matter of how many jobs AI will eliminate. Though AI leaders keep repeating over and over that the technology will lead to newer, different jobs and an economic windfall for everybody, they can’t say what jobs it would create or how it will economically benefit everyday people.

articles.title: London Film Fest Gets Concrete – Literally, and More Than Once!
articles.summary: The 2026 lineup, including several movies with "concrete" in their title, made for "hilarious and quite confusing program meetings," shares fest director Kristy Matheson.
body: Last year, all sorts of birds were seen flying through the movies in the lineup of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF). This year, the festival is getting concrete – literally, and more than once.
In fact, three feature films in the LFF 2026 lineup have the word “concrete” in the title.

Could the fact that a building material is featuring prominently in several film titles tell us something about the state of cinema and filmmakers’ current priorities? “The idea of getting back to something elemental, that’s something that really started to emerge in the program,” offers Matheson.
So, without further ado, here is a closer look at the three “concrete” titles in the LFF 2026 program.

articles.title: ‘Artificial’ Review: Luca Guadagnino Has Made the Real Sequel to ‘The Social Network’ — a Brain-Spinning Tech-Geek Docudrama, Brilliantly Acted by Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov
articles.summary: "Artificial" is a brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history, that focuses on the founders of OpenAI, notably its CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). But the tale it tells is much larger than that.
body: It charts the invention and corporate rise of AI, taking off from the cathartically topical question: If we don't control AI, who will?

By 2012, Ilya and Hinton have comes up with an AI model that’s developed enough to place in an auction. Within five seconds, there’s a bid on the table for $20 million, and the two decide to sell their knowledge to Google. They will set up a lab there, working independently, and have their research funded. This works for a while, but John (Chris O’Dowd), the Google executive in charge, doesn’t really get where they’re going with AI. He’s not onboard with the vision of it. Sam Altman, a rising star of Silicon Valley, is.

articles.title: ‘Ba’s Book’: How Making the Heartfelt Hybrid Film Exploring Trauma Brought a Family Closer Together
articles.summary: Ashley Duong's cinematic journey, which screens at the London Film Fest, uncovers painful memories that her father long kept from his family about escaping the Vietnam War and living as a refugee in Iran.
body: In Anh Duong’s memoir Dear Da-Lê: A Father’s Memoir of the Vietnam War and the Iranian Revolution, published in 2024, the author recounts his experiences and family trauma for his daughter Ashley – from his childhood near Huế, Vietnam and escaping the Vietnam War to living as a refugee during the 1970s revolution in Iran, and arriving in Canada in 1980.

Written and directed by Ashley Da-Lê Duong, it world premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and is now celebrating its international premiere during the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival, where it will screen on Oct. 8 and 9.

This is how press notes about Ba’s Book set up the film: “Returning to her ancestral village, [Ashley] collaborates with her father and relatives to film participatory re-creations of their past. A true hybrid of live-action and documentary, Ba’s Book offers a disarming look at how a family moves forward from divisions caused by displacement and war.”
Ahead of the London screenings, Ashley Duong discussed her experience making Ba’s Book and how it changed her relationship with her family with THR.
